assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Resistance
items.clue: Quantity proportional to the length of a wire and to 1/A.

items.label: Series
items.clue: Arrangement in which a kettle element and its cable carry the same current.

items.label: Ohm's law
items.clue: Special case in which V/I stays constant: a straight I–V line through the origin.

items.label: Resistivity
items.clue: Property ρ that depends only on the material and its temperature, not on its shape.

questions.stem: A silver wire and a copper wire are connected in series, so they carry the same current. Silver has 5.9 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³; copper has 8.5 × 10²⁸. The silver wire has twice the cross-sectional area of the copper wire. What is the ratio (drift speed in silver) / (drift speed in copper)?
questions.explanation: v = I/(nAe), and I and e are the same, so v ∝ 1/(nA). Ratio = (8.5/5.9) ÷ 2 = 0.72.

questions.stem: A battery of emf 12 V drives a steady current of 40 A through a starter motor for 1.5 s. How much energy does the battery transfer to the charge that passes through it in this time?
questions.explanation: Charge: q = It = 40 × 1.5 = 60 C. Each coulomb gains 12 J, so energy = emf × q = 12 × 60 = 720 J.

questions.stem: A student investigates whether a length of metal wire obeys Ohm's law. At the highest currents, V/I is clearly larger than at low currents. What is the best change to the method?

options.text: Use a voltmeter with a higher resolution, so the pd readings are more precise.
Take each reading twice, once with the supply reversed, and average the results.
Extend the range to even higher currents, so that more points lie on the graph.
Keep currents small or use a water bath, so the wire's temperature is constant.

questions.explanation: Ohm's law applies at constant temperature. Small currents (or a water bath) stop the wire heating, so V/I stays constant for an ohmic wire.

questions.stem: A copper wire is connected across an ideal battery. The wire is then cooled from 60 °C to 20 °C; its length and cross-sectional area change by negligible amounts. How do the wire's resistance and the current in it change as it cools?

options.text: The resistance increases, and the current decreases.
The resistance and the current both remain the same.
The resistance decreases; the current does not vary.
The resistance decreases, and the current increases.

questions.stem: A steady current of 0.25 A flows in a 24 Ω resistor for 2.0 minutes. How much energy is dissipated in the resistor?
questions.explanation: Power = I²R = 0.25² × 24 = 1.5 W. Energy = power × time = 1.5 W × 120 s = 180 J.

questions.stem: A wire consists of two sections made of the same metal and joined end to end. The diameter of section 2 is half the diameter of section 1. The wire carries a steady current, which is the same in both sections. What is the ratio v₂/v₁ of the drift speed of the free electrons in section 2 to that in section 1?
questions.explanation: The current, the number density and the charge are the same in both sections, so drift speed ∝ 1/A. Half the diameter gives (½)² = ¼ of the area, so the electrons drift 4 times as fast.

questions.stem: A steady current of 0.50 A flows through a small electric motor for 2.0 minutes. In this time, 360 J of energy is transferred from electrical energy to other forms in the motor. What is the potential difference across the motor?
Predict first. What is the origin of the electrical resistance of a metal wire?

options.text: Free electrons collide with the vibrating lattice ions, transferring energy to them.
Some of the free electrons are absorbed by the metal atoms, so fewer leave than enter.
The electrons rub against the surface of the wire, like water flowing along a pipe.
The electrons bump into one another as they crowd through the wire.

questions.stem: A copper cable has length 5.0 m and diameter 1.0 mm. The resistivity of copper is 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What is the resistance of the cable?

The potential difference across an ohmic resistor is increased so that the current in the resistor becomes three times as large. What is the ratio of the new power dissipated in the resistor, P₂, to the original power, P₁?
questions.explanation: The resistor is ohmic, so R is unchanged. P = I²R: tripling I multiplies P by 3² = 9.

questions.stem: A copper wire of diameter 1.6 mm carries a steady current of 3.0 A. Measurements show that its free electrons, each with a charge of magnitude e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, drift at 1.1 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. What is the number of free electrons per unit volume in the copper?
Predict first. A cell has an emf of 1.5 V. What does this mean?

options.text: The cell holds a store of 1.5 C of charge, which it releases into the circuit.
The cell pushes each coulomb of charge around the circuit with a force of 1.5 N.
For each coulomb passing through the cell, 1.5 J is transferred to electrical energy.
The cell drives a current of 1.5 A through any circuit connected to it.
